title: Even Down to Ten Recitations
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Q: Among the forty-eight great vows of Amitabha Buddha, the Eighteenth Vow is: “If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions who sincerely and joyfully believe and wish to be born in my land, even down to ten recitations, should fail to be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment — excepting only those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the true Dharma.” (The Buddha Speaks of the Infinite Life Sutra). inline.s: Q: Among the forty-eight great vows of Amitabha Buddha, the Eighteenth Vow is:

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions who sincerely and joyfully believe and wish to be born in my land, even down to ten recitations, should fail to be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment — excepting only those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the true Dharma.”

(The Buddha Speaks of the Infinite Life Sutra). In this passage of the vow, the four words “even down to ten recitations” are of the utmost importance, for they are the condition for rebirth. May I ask, what is the specific meaning of “even down to ten recitations”?

[The five grave offenses] The five rebellious acts: five kinds of evil that run utterly counter to reason — namely, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the harmonious Sangha. Because these five are acts of extreme wickedness, committing any one of them causes one to fall into the Avīci (Uninterrupted) Hell, so they are also called “the karma of uninterrupted retribution.”
A:
In the Eighteenth Vow,
“even down to ten recitations”
is
“even at the point of death, ten recitations in unbroken succession, calling my name”
, in abbreviated form. Regarding this,
the sage of practice and realization, Master Daochuo, clearly instructed in his Anle Ji (Collection on Peace and Joy):
If there are sentient beings who, even if they have committed evil all their lives,
at the point of death, with ten recitations in unbroken succession
, calling my name,
if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Here, Master Daochuo gives a precise explanation of the meaning of “even down to ten recitations” in the Eighteenth Vow:
at the point of death, ten recitations in unbroken succession, calling my name.
(For details, see
Master Daochuo's Pure Land Teachings
Therefore, in the Eighteenth Vow,
the specific meaning of “even down to ten recitations” is: even at the point of death, ten recitations in unbroken succession, calling the Buddha's name.
As for what “ten recitations in unbroken succession” means, and
the conditions for rebirth, the sage of practice and realization, Master Tanluan, instructed
(for details, see
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teachings
Without the intermingling of other thoughts
(without the admixture of delusive thoughts),
mind following upon mind in succession
(mind succeeding mind),
even down to ten recitations — this is called “ten recitations in unbroken succession.”
With ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death, one attains rebirth.
Regarding
how to practice
so as to surely attain
rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss
, Master Shandao instructed in On the Exclusive and Mixed Practice of the Pure Karma:
Unbroken succession means birth.
If one can
keep thought after thought in unbroken succession,
taking
the whole of life as the term
(one who practices this way throughout life) —
then of ten, ten are born; of a hundred, a hundred are born.
May all people reflect well upon this: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must
exert your mind and restrain yourself
(spur yourself on and discipline yourself)
never ceasing by day or night
(never stopping the unbroken succession of thoughts day or night),
so that when the former thought ends, the next thought is born at once.
Forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of the Dharma,
and finally attaining Buddhahood,
would that not be splendid!
Of this instruction,
Master Yinguang, a reincarnation of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva,
praised it most highly:
Master Shandao is an incarnation of Amitabha,
possessing great spiritual powers and great wisdom. In broadly expounding the Pure Land, he does not esteem the profound and mysterious, but only, in what is genuine and plain,
teaches people to practice.
As for
his On the Exclusive and Mixed Practice, its benefit is boundless
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, “Reply to a Layman of Yongjia and His Brothers”)
As for the conditions of rebirth, Master Shandao instructed in his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra,
saying:
If I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions who call my name and wish to be born in my land,
down to ten recitations
(down to ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death),
if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
[Down to ten recitations]
The phrase “down to ten recitations” spoken of here, read together with Master Shandao's instruction above,
“thought after thought in unbroken succession, taking the whole of life as the term,”
makes it clearly evident that this is
“from above, exhausting one whole life
(one lifetime)
in unbroken succession, down to
ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death
in abbreviated form. For Master Shandao has already clearly said:
“thought after thought in unbroken succession, taking the whole of life as the term,”
and
“thought after thought in unbroken succession, taking the whole of life as the term”
is precisely for the sake of making unbroken succession into a settled habit,
so as to ensure ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death
If one recites the Buddha's name in ordinary times but does not recite at the point of death, or if one does recite at the point of death but with a scattered mind, neither of these is
“thought after thought in unbroken succession, taking the whole of life as the term.”
Therefore, the meaning of “down to ten recitations” is
“down to ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death.”
This kind of concise expression is everywhere in classical Chinese prose. Hence
“down to ten recitations; if they are not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
means:
down to
ten recitations at the point of death; with unbroken succession, one is born.
[Ten recitations] Reciting ten utterances of the Buddha's name.
[Unbroken succession becoming a settled habit] Through constant repetition and practice, making unbroken succession into second nature.

Master Shandao is Amitabha Buddha returned, so his words are Amitabha Buddha's words. How one may attain rebirth should of course be based on his words — this is the authoritative testimony of the sages. Those who recite the Buddha's name must engrave this on their hearts, believing it all the more, and relying on it all the more.
Editor's note: In Master Shandao's time, after the teaching of three generations of patriarchs — Master Tanluan, Master Daochuo, and Master Shandao —
“ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death is the condition for rebirth”
had already become the common understanding of those who recited the Buddha's name, and indeed their most basic common knowledge.
Therefore,
“down to ten recitations; if they are not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”
clearly means:
down to ten recitations at the point of death; with unbroken succession, one is born.
Unless one is a complete layman who understands nothing, or a malicious person who slanders the Dharma with ulterior motives, one would never distort
“down to ten recitations; if they are not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”

into “reciting the Buddha's name ten times with a scattered mind in ordinary times, and one will be born.” So Master Shandao adopted the concise expression “down to ten recitations,” making the whole sentence brief and well-formed, pleasant to read aloud, and easy to memorize — this was the customary style of classical writing.
Moreover, Master Shandao clearly explained:
“Unbroken succession means birth. If one can
keep thought after thought in unbroken succession, taking the whole of life as the term
, then of ten, ten are born; of a hundred, a hundred are born.
May all people reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must
exert one's mind and restrain oneself
(spur oneself on and discipline oneself)
never ceasing by day or night
(never stopping the unbroken succession of thoughts day or night),
so that when the former thought ends, the next thought is born at once. Forever enjoying the unconditioned bliss of the Dharma, and finally attaining Buddhahood — would that not be splendid!
(For details, see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teachings
If “reciting the Buddha's name ten times with a scattered mind in ordinary times, and one will be born,” why would Master Shandao need to say
“unbroken succession means birth”
And why
need he say
“thought after thought in unbroken succession, taking the whole of life as the term”
? And why
need he say
“whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must exert one's mind, restrain oneself, and never cease by day or night”
? Therefore, when Huijing, Jingzong, and others take
“down to ten recitations; if they are not born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment”

and distort it into “reciting the Buddha's name ten times with a scattered mind in ordinary times, and one will be born” (and then loudly advocate that “calling the name guarantees birth”), they are completely mistaken.
Master Yongming, a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha,
regarding the conditions of rebirth,
in his Wanshan Tonggui Ji (Collection on the Convergence of Ten Thousand Good Deeds)
instructed:
one must use a mind of unbroken succession to accomplish the ten recitations at the point of death.
Master Yongming said:
If one's words and deeds do not match
(if words and deeds do not accord),
if one's power of faith is slight and weak, lacking
a mind of unbroken succession,

and harboring a mind given to repeated interruption — if one relies on this and grows lax, hoping at the point of death to be born, one will merely be veiled by karmic obstructions, and may find it hard to meet good friends; pressed by wind and fire, one's right mindfulness will not be achieved. Why is this so? The present is the cause, the point of death is the fruit; the cause must be real, and then the fruit will not be empty. If one wishes to
accomplish the ten recitations at the point of death,
one should make preparations beforehand, gather merit together, and dedicate it to that moment
(dedicate it to the time of death)
so that thought after thought is not deficient; then there will be nothing to worry about.

[Master Yongming is also a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha] Master Yongming is a reincarnation of Amitabha Buddha, so Master Yongming's birthday, the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, is observed as Amitabha Buddha's birthday. Of Master Yongming, Master Yinguang praised:
“Master Yongming is an incarnation of Amitabha Buddha. With great kindness and great compassion, he opens and transforms sentient beings.”
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
“Dharma Words of Instruction at the World Buddhist Laymen's Association”)

[Accomplish the ten recitations at the point of death] To accomplish ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death. [Prepare the ford and bridge beforehand] “Jinliang” means a ford and a bridge; “prepare the ford and bridge beforehand” means to make preparations in advance.

This instruction of Master Yongming is entirely consistent with Master Shandao's instruction, and entirely consistent with the instructions of the sages of practice and realization, Master Tanluan and Master Daochuo.
Q: The great British scholar of religion, Max Müller
(Max Müller)

) and others translate the Eighteenth Vow as follows: “Bhagavan, when I attain bodhi, if the sentient beings of countless, innumerable Buddha lands, after hearing my name, I will cause their minds to think of my Buddha land, and I will cause their wish for rebirth, accumulated through good roots, to be fulfilled — even if they have only ten thoughts (thoughts of rebirth), if they are not born into my Buddha land, then I will not become the supreme, perfect enlightenment. Excepting those who commit the five grave offenses and those who hinder and slander the true Dharma.” They interpret “even down to ten recitations” as “even if they have only ten thoughts (thoughts of rebirth).” Is it correct to understand “even down to ten recitations” in this way?
A: This passage of the vow in The Buddha Speaks of the Infinite Life Sutra reads:

“If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions who sincerely and joyfully believe and wish to be born in my land, even down to ten recitations, should fail to be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment — excepting only those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the true Dharma.”

Müller and the others' translation takes the words at face value without understanding their meaning. They do not know at all the inner significance of “even down to ten recitations”; a hairsbreadth of error leads to a thousand miles of mistake. Those who do not comprehend the Buddhadharma and the principle of rebirth, and who have not attained realization, have no qualification whatsoever to translate this passage of the vow. The idiom “searching for a steed by following a picture” describes exactly such a layman who takes words at face value: in his book On Discerning Horses, Bo Le wrote that “a high forehead, bright eyes, and large hooves make a fine horse.” Once, Bo Le's son took the book and went out to identify a horse. He saw a toad and said to his father, “I have found a thousand-li steed — it meets all the other conditions, only its hooves are a bit too small!” Bo Le knew his son was foolish, and was so exasperated that he laughed, saying, “The horse you have caught loves to hop too much — it cannot be ridden!” That is why in our country the translation of Buddhist scriptures is handled with great care, with a dedicated translation bureau. Within the bureau there are the chief translator, the interpreter, the verifier of meaning, and the polisher of prose. Moreover, the one serving as chief translator must be a Tripitaka master — a bhikṣu thoroughly versed in the sutra-pitaka, the vinaya-pitaka, and the abhidharma-pitaka.

Buddhist scriptures are not a study of mere words; they are classics that guide practice toward the attainment of realization. Only one who thoroughly understands practice and has attained realization can grasp their true meaning and is qualified to translate them. Imagine, if a peerless manual of martial arts were explained by a scholar who had never practiced martial arts — what sort of result would that be? So when someone who knows a little Sanskrit sets out to translate the Buddhist scriptures, he is bound to make the great joke of mistaking a toad for a thousand-li steed!
In this very sutra (The Buddha Speaks of the Infinite Life Sutra) there is also this passage:
“Ascending the Way is boundless beyond compare
(once born into the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the speed of one's ascension on the path and the stage one attains are beyond all comparison),
easy to go to, yet no one goes
(and yet this practice, so easy to accomplish, is seldom carried out in earnest),
its land turns no one away
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss refuses no one who would be born there),
and one is drawn along by one's own natural inclination

(those sentient beings who have not been born into the Land of Ultimate Bliss follow the delusions of their final moments and naturally go to be reborn in the six realms).” If, according to Müller and the others' translation, “even if they have only ten thoughts (thoughts of rebirth)” they will certainly be born, then how could there be
“no one”

[Easy to go to, yet no one goes] Here “easy to go to” is spoken relative to other Dharma gates. Take the Chan school, for instance: one must pass through the myriad thoughts returning to one (which corresponds to the Pure Land school's one mind undisturbed), then the one returning to nothingness, then seeing one's nature and realizing the mind; and only after the work of sustaining and nurturing, and cutting off all afflictions completely, can one end birth and death and escape the cycle of rebirth. But the Pure Land Dharma gate requires only ten recitations in unbroken succession at the point of death to be born into the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, thereby ending birth and death and escaping the cycle of rebirth — hence it is called “easy to go to.”
Moreover, the World-Honored One, in speaking of the three grades of birth in this sutra, says that one should:
“single-mindedly and exclusively recite Amitabha Buddha's name.”
If “even if they have only ten thoughts (thoughts of rebirth)” they will certainly be born, then what need would there be for “single-minded exclusive recitation”?
There would be no need even to recite the Buddha's name at all — only ten thoughts of rebirth would suffice! Then what Buddha-recitation Dharma gate would there be?
Moreover, the World-Honored One (Śākyamuni Buddha) also enjoined in this sutra:
“Practice as it has been taught.”
(The Buddha Speaks of the Infinite Life Sutra says:
“Having heard this sutra's Dharma, rejoice and believe with delight, receive, uphold, recite, and
practice as it has been taught

) If “even if they have only ten thoughts (thoughts of rebirth)” they will certainly be born, then what need would there be for any practice? And what would “as it has been taught” in the World-Honored One's words “practice as it has been taught” mean?
Moreover, the World-Honored One also encouraged in this sutra,
saying:
“Though in this one life there is toil and hardship, in but an instant one will later be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss without limit.”
If “even if they have only ten thoughts (thoughts of rebirth)” they will certainly be born, then what toil and hardship would there be?

In past foreign-affairs work, there was once an interpreter who translated the idiom “to have a well-thought-out plan” (literally “to have a bamboo fully formed in one's breast”) as “to have a bamboo in one's chest,” leaving the audience baffled. This joke should serve as a warning bell to those who, knowing a little Sanskrit, would set out to translate the Buddhist scriptures.
To those who think that, having a Sanskrit text, they may retranslate the Buddhist scriptures, Master Yinguang instructed:

“A person should value self-knowledge and not presumptuously utter extravagant boasts. Looking at your doubts and arguments, you regard the translation of scriptures as utterly without difficulty, as though one needed only to know a foreign language to be qualified as a translator. Yet if you set such a person to translate scriptures, it would be the same as one who does not understand the foreign tongue at all. You wish to rely on a Sanskrit text, but a Sanskrit text is not cast of iron. One must possess the discerning eye of wisdom to distinguish whether the meaning of a Sanskrit text is accurate, or whether it has long been corrupted by errors in transmission, before one may translate scriptures. Moreover, this cannot be accomplished by one person alone; hence within the translation bureau there must be many learned masters — some who translate the text, and some who verify its meaning. Those who join the translation bureau are by no means people wholly ignorant of the Buddhadharma. You treat the translation of scriptures entirely as translating words for foreigners. This is just like a literate man who recognizes every character but, faced with the profound writings of the sages, has no idea what they mean. Such presumptuous talk — never utter it again.”
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang,
“Reply to Layman Wang Zili, Letter One”)

Translation: A person should value self-knowledge and not presumptuously utter extravagant boasts. Looking at your discussion, you regard the translation of Buddhist scriptures as entirely without difficulty, as though one needed only to know a foreign language to qualify as a translator. If you set such a person to translate scriptures, it would be the same as one who does not understand the foreign tongue at all. You wish to translate according to a Sanskrit text, but a Sanskrit text is not cast of iron (meaning: it is not that a Sanskrit text, over the long course of its transmission, has not the slightest error, or that the meaning of each word is rigid and does not change with the combination of words and phrases). One must be able to truly distinguish the meaning of a Sanskrit text, and possess the discerning eye of wisdom to judge whether the Sanskrit text one intends to translate is correct and free of error, or whether it has been corrupted over long transmission — only then may one translate scriptures. Yet this is not something one person can accomplish; therefore, within the translation bureau there must be many learned masters (people who are simultaneously well-versed in Sanskrit and Chinese, thoroughly versed in the three baskets, and who have both practice and realization). There are those who translate the text, and those who verify its meaning. Those who participate in the translation bureau are by no means people wholly ignorant of the Buddhadharma. You treat the translation of scriptures entirely as translating words for foreigners. This is just like a literate man who recognizes every character, but faced with the profound writings of the sages, has no idea at all what they mean. (This is also like thinking that, knowing English and a bit of advanced mathematics, one could translate Einstein's theory of relativity into Chinese — truly not knowing the height of heaven or the depth of earth!) Never again utter such presumptuous talk of wanting to translate the Buddhist scriptures.
